# Problem Statement

**Artifact Type:** Problem Statement
**Flow Step:** 03 — Define Target Problem
**Business Phase:** Problem Discovery
**Owner:** PM-001
**Status:** Draft — pending CEO-001 and UX Researcher (UXR-001) review
**Version:** 1.0
**Date:** 2026-01-01 (run date placeholder)
**Inputs:** Idea Brief v1.0 (step 01), Initial Opportunity Hypothesis v1.0 (step 02)

---

## 1. Purpose

This artifact converts the reframed, B2B-first opportunity from step 02 into a
specific, testable customer problem with a measurable desired outcome, per this
step's gate criterion. It exists to be falsifiable in Problem Discovery/Market
Validation (steps 04-09) — if the interviews in those steps contradict this
statement, this document gets revised, not defended.

I am carrying forward step 02's strategic reframing as the working boundary: this
Problem Statement is scoped to the **publisher/rights-holder segment (A)** as
primary and the **indie-author segment (B)** as secondary, with the **consumer
reader segment (C)** explicitly excluded from problem scope at this stage (see
Section 5). This is a decision inherited from CEO-001's step-02 framing, not a new
PM-001 decision — I am applying it, and flagging where I'd want it re-tested.

---

## 2. Primary Problem Statement (Segment A — Publishers/Rights-Holders)

> **Bengali-language publishing houses and rights-holders who want to bring
> English-language backlist or licensed titles to Bengali-speaking readers
> currently face a translation production process that is slow (multi-month
> per title, human-translator-dependent), expensive relative to the commercial
> ceiling of most Bengali-market book sales, and difficult to scale across a
> catalog — which causes them to translate only a small fraction of the
> English-language titles they hold or could license, leaving demand for those
> titles unmet in the Bengali market.**

### 2.1 Problem components (made specific and measurable)

| Dimension | Current state (hypothesized) | Measurable pain signal to validate in discovery |
|---|---|---|
| **Speed** | Human literary translation of a full-length book typically takes multiple months per title, per translator | Target: validate actual turnaround time publishers report today (in weeks/months) via direct interview, step 05 |
| **Cost** | Per-title human translation cost is a meaningful fixed cost that must be justified against expected Bengali-market sales for that specific title | Target: validate the minimum expected sales volume a publisher requires to green-light a translation today, and how many titles fall below that bar |
| **Catalog scale** | Publishers/rights-holders can only translate a small share of eligible titles per year given translator capacity and budget | Target: validate ratio of "titles publisher holds/could license" to "titles publisher actually translates to Bengali per year" |
| **Quality risk of faster alternatives** | Publishers who might try MT-assisted translation today have no trusted, book-length-consistent, editorially-reviewed workflow — they either avoid MT entirely or use it informally without quality assurance | Target: validate whether publishers have tried any MT-assisted approach and why they did/didn't adopt it |

**ASSUMPTION (to validate in step 05 interviews):** the binding constraint on
publishers is *not* readers' willingness to buy Bengali translations — it is
publishers' internal cost/capacity ceiling for producing them. If discovery
interviews (step 05) contradict this — e.g., publishers report the real constraint
is weak Bengali-market sales interest, not production cost/speed — this Problem
Statement must be revised before proceeding to step 07.

### 2.2 Desired Outcome (Segment A)

> A publisher/rights-holder can take an English-language title from
> license-secured to a publishable, editorially-approved Bengali edition in
> **materially less time and at materially lower cost than their current
> all-human vendor pipeline**, at a quality bar their own editorial standards
> accept — enabling them to translate a **larger share of their eligible
> catalog** than they do today.

**Success is measurable as:**
- Turnaround time per title (target: reduction vs. publisher's current baseline —
  exact target % TBD after step 05 baseline interviews; **not yet quantifiable**,
  flagged as open question below).
- Cost per title (target: reduction vs. publisher's current baseline — same caveat).
- Publisher editorial acceptance rate of MT+human-reviewed output without
  requiring a full manual re-translation (this is the real quality bar — not
  "reads correctly" but "an editor accepts it as a base to review rather than
  discards it and translates from scratch").
- Number/share of a publisher's eligible catalog they choose to translate in a
  given period, before vs. after adoption (a longer-cycle, post-launch metric).

---

## 3. Secondary Problem Statement (Segment B — Indie/Self-Publishing Authors)

> **English-language independent authors who want a Bengali edition of their
> book to reach Bengali-speaking readers are currently priced out of
> professional human literary translation for a single title, and have no
> accessible, quality-assured alternative — so most self-published English
> titles are never made available in Bengali at all.**

### 3.1 Desired Outcome (Segment B)
> An indie author can obtain a Bengali edition of their book at a price and
> turnaround appropriate to a single-title, self-funded budget, with enough
> quality assurance (human-reviewed, not raw MT output) that they are willing
> to publish and put their name behind it.

**Success is measurable as:** conversion rate of authors from "interested" to
"paid," price point cleared, and post-delivery author satisfaction/willingness
to recommend. This segment is retained as a **secondary, faster-to-interview**
validation target (step 05), not as the segment the MVP is built around — per
step 02's sequencing, Segment A's problem gets validated first because it has
the cleaner rights path and revenue model.

---

## 4. Root Cause (why this problem exists, not just what it looks like)

**INFERENCE**, drawn from Idea Brief/step-02 reasoning, to be tested rather than
assumed true:

1. English-Bengali is a lower-resource language pair in mainstream MT/LLM
   training relative to major European and other major Asian languages, so
   general-purpose MT tools, while free, have not historically been trusted for
   long-form literary use without heavy human correction — leaving publishers
   dependent on slow, fully-manual translation as the only trusted path.
2. No existing vendor appears to combine (a) MT-assisted speed, (b)
   book-length consistency tooling (glossary/terminology/character-name
   continuity across chapters), and (c) a managed editorial-review workflow
   publishers can trust — publishers currently must choose between "fully
   manual and trusted" or "fast but unmanaged and untrusted," with nothing
   between.

This root-cause framing is what makes the problem specific enough to design
against: the target is not "translation is hard," it is **"there is no
trusted, book-length-consistent, editorially-managed middle option between
slow-manual and fast-unmanaged for EN→BN book translation."** If step 05/06
research finds a competitor already occupies this middle position credibly,
this Problem Statement's differentiation claim must be revisited (see Section
6, open questions).

---

## 5. Explicit Exclusions (what this problem statement is NOT about)

- **Segment C (individual consumer readers)** is explicitly excluded from this
  problem statement's scope at this stage. Rationale (inherited from step 02):
  a consumer-facing product translating in-copyright English books without
  rights clearance is a legal-risk problem, not a product problem, and solving
  it would require a rights-cleared catalog this company does not yet have.
  This exclusion should be revisited only after Segment A validates and
  produces a licensed content pipeline (see step 02, Section 2.2).
- **General-purpose short-form translation** (e.g., casual text, non-book
  content) is out of scope — the problem is specifically long-form,
  book-length, published-quality translation, where general MT tools are
  weakest and where a workflow/consistency layer has room to add value.
- **Bengali-to-English** (the reverse direction) is out of scope for this
  problem statement; the Idea Brief and step-02 framing are English-to-Bengali
  only. Worth flagging as a possible future expansion (step 77), not now.
- **Non-Bengali target languages** are out of scope; no claim is made here
  about this problem generalizing to other low-resource language pairs, though
  it may (flagged as a future strategic question, not this step's concern).

---

## 6. Evidence Basis, Confidence, and Open Questions

**Evidence basis:** This Problem Statement is built entirely on the Idea
Brief's and Initial Opportunity Hypothesis's inference and general industry
knowledge — **no direct customer interviews, no live market research, and no
technical MT-quality benchmark have been conducted yet** (no research/browser
tools are connected this run; see Required Integration block below). This is
appropriate for step 03 (defining what to test), but this statement's
confidence must not be overstated.

**Confidence: MEDIUM.** The problem is logically coherent, specific, and
measurable in structure (turnaround time, cost, editorial acceptance rate,
catalog-share). It is *not yet* evidence-backed by real publisher input.

**Open questions to resolve before step 07 Market Assessment is finalized:**
1. Do real Bengali publishers report cost/speed/capacity as their binding
   constraint on translation volume — or is it something else (market demand
   uncertainty, distribution, printing/logistics)? (step 05)
2. What EN→BN MT/LLM output quality is actually achievable today for literary
   text, and how many editorial hours per book does it currently require to
   reach publishable quality? This determines whether the cost/speed
   improvement in Section 2.2 is even achievable. (CTO-001 benchmark, flagged
   in step 02, needed before this Problem Statement's numeric targets can be
   set)
3. Does any existing vendor already occupy the "MT-assisted + managed
   editorial + book-consistency" middle position described in Section 4? (step
   06/08 competitive analysis)
4. Is the publisher segment's real problem catalog-wide (many titles, capacity
   constrained) or title-specific (a few high-value titles, quality
   constrained)? These imply different MVP value loops and should be
   distinguished in step 05 interviews.

```text
Required Integration:
Tool: Web/browser research and/or direct customer interview scheduling
Capability: Verified publisher/author interview data, competitor landscape
  confirmation, and independent validation of the root-cause and problem-scale
  claims in Sections 4 and 6
Why Needed: This Problem Statement's specificity claims (turnaround time,
  cost baseline, catalog-share) cannot be quantified without real publisher
  input, and no research or outreach tool is connected this run
Alternative: All quantitative targets are left as "TBD after step 05 baseline
  interviews" rather than fabricated; qualitative structure of the problem is
  stated with explicit ASSUMPTION/INFERENCE labeling
Human Escalation: Founder/UXR-001 to schedule and conduct real publisher and
  indie-author interviews (5-10 per segment, per step 02's recommendation)
  before step 07 is finalized
```

---

## 7. Traceability

- Traces to Idea Brief (step 01), Section 3 Segment A/B, and Section 5 known
  risks (copyright, commoditization).
- Traces to Initial Opportunity Hypothesis (step 02), Section 2.2 (strategic
  reframing decision) and Section 5 (feasibility conditions) — this Problem
  Statement inherits and operationalizes that reframing; it does not
  re-litigate it.
- No prior Decision Memory or Assumption Register entries exist yet (first
  Problem Discovery artifact in this company's history) — this document
  becomes the baseline for future assumption checks.

---

## 8. Next Steps / Handoff

1. **UXR-001**: design and run discovery interviews (step 05) with 5-10
   publisher contacts (Segment A) and 5-10 indie authors (Segment B) against
   the specific questions in Section 6, to convert this statement's
   ASSUMPTION/INFERENCE claims into FACT or revise them.
2. **CEO-001**: review this Problem Statement for consistency with the step-02
   strategic reframing before it's used to gate step 04 (ICP definition).
3. **CTO-001**: run the EN→BN literary MT quality benchmark (flagged in step
   02) in parallel — its output directly determines whether Section 2.2's
   desired-outcome targets are achievable at all.
4. Proceed to step 04 (ICP/Persona Draft) using Segment A as primary and
   Segment B as secondary, pending no contradicting findings from step 05.

**Loop condition (per this step's spec):** if step 05 interviews reveal this
problem statement is vague, wrong about the binding constraint (Section 2.1's
assumption), or not actually a top-3 pain point for real publishers, PM-001
will revise this Problem Statement before proceeding to step 04 rather than
carrying a shaky foundation forward.

claims.text: Publishers' binding constraint on EN->BN book translation volume is cost/speed/capacity, not reader demand or distribution.
The real constraint tested in step 05 interviews may differ from this hypothesis; this statement is falsifiable and will be revised if contradicted.

No existing vendor currently combines MT-assisted speed, book-length consistency tooling, and managed editorial review for EN->BN translation, leaving a gap between slow-manual and fast-unmanaged options.
Segment C (consumer readers) is excluded from problem scope pending a rights-cleared content pipeline, inheriting the step-02 strategic reframing decision.

Human literary translation of a full book typically takes multiple months and represents a meaningful fixed per-title cost for publishers; figure is general industry knowledge, not independently verified this run.
Quantitative success targets (turnaround %, cost %) should remain 'TBD' until step 05 baseline interviews establish real publisher baselines, rather than being estimated without evidence.
This Problem Statement is scoped to Segment A (publishers) as primary and Segment B (indie authors) as secondary, applying the step-02 CEO reframing rather than re-opening it.

open_questions: Do real publishers report cost/speed/capacity as the binding constraint on translation volume, or is it something else (market demand, distribution, printing)?
What EN->BN MT/LLM literary translation quality is achievable today, and how many editorial hours per book does it require?
Does an existing vendor already occupy the 'MT-assisted + managed editorial + consistency tooling' middle position this problem statement assumes is open?
Is the publisher problem catalog-wide (capacity-constrained across many titles) or title-specific (quality-constrained on a few high-value titles)?
